usamts-2015-r1-01.title: Columns increase; use divisibility to pick the rule
usamts-2015-r1-01.body:
**Columns increase.** In a $2\times2$ square, if $a < c$ then $b < d$ under either rule ($d = b + (c - a)$ or $d = b\cdot\frac ca$). Since $9 < 11$ in column 2, every number in row 1 is less than the one below it, and similarly for the other pairs of rows ($2 < 16$ in column 5; $10 < 15 < 20$ in column 1). The implication also runs right-to-left, since both rules are symmetric, so **every column increases downward**.

**Choosing the rule.** For a square with three entries known, the fourth is $b + c - a$ (additive) or $\frac{bc}{a}$ (multiplicative), and the multiplicative option only exists when $a \mid bc$. For example, in rows 4–5, columns 1–2: $15, x / 20, 36$ gives $x = 31$ or $x = 27$. Working through the grid with these two options and the increasing columns, trial and error quickly settles every square:
$$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|}\hline 3 & 9 & 12 & 6 & 1\\\hline 5 & 11 & 14 & 7 & 2\\\hline 10 & 22 & 28 & 21 & 16\\\hline 15 & 27 & 33 & 26 & 21\\\hline 20 & 36 & 44 & 37 & 32\\\hline\end{array}$$

**Check** (each $2\times2$ square, rule used): e.g. $3, 9 / 5, 11$: $3 + 11 = 9 + 5$; $9, 12 / 11, 14$: additive; $12, 6 / 14, 7$: $12\cdot7 = 6\cdot14$; $6, 1 / 7, 2$: additive; $5, 11 / 10, 22$: $5\cdot22 = 11\cdot10$; $14, 7 / 28, 21$: additive; $7, 2 / 21, 16$: additive; $15, 27 / 20, 36$: $15\cdot36 = 27\cdot20$; $26, 21 / 37, 32$: additive. All 16 squares satisfy one of the rules, and a computer search confirms this is the only solution.

usamts-2015-r1-02.title: Compare with $(x-1)(x-10)(x-100)$
usamts-2015-r1-02.body:
Expanding the second equation, $bc - abc + ab + ac = 110$; adding $abc = 1000$ gives
$$ab + bc + ca = 1110.$$
So $a, b, c$ are the roots of
$$f(x) = (x - a)(x - b)(x - c) = x^3 - dx^2 + 1110x - 1000,\qquad d = a + b + c.$$
Compare with
$$g(x) = (x - 1)(x - 10)(x - 100) = x^3 - 111x^2 + 1110x - 1000.$$
Then $g(x) - f(x) = (d - 111)x^2$.

Since $0 < a < 1$, all three factors of $g(a)$ are negative, so $g(a) < 0$. As $f(a) = 0$, $(d - 111)a^2 = g(a) < 0$, so $d < 111$. Hence for every $x \ne 0$, $g(x) - f(x) < 0$; in particular
$$g(b) = g(b) - f(b) < 0,\qquad g(c) = g(c) - f(c) < 0.$$
For positive $x$, $g(x) < 0$ exactly when $0 < x < 1$ or $10 < x < 100$. So $b, c \in (0, 1) \cup (10, 100)$.

Finally $bc = \frac{1000}{a} > 1000$. If $c < 1$ then $b > 1000$, impossible; so $c > 10$ and therefore $10 < c < 100$ (and likewise for $b$). ∎

usamts-2015-r1-03.title: The difference of areas is affine
usamts-2015-r1-03.body:
For $Q$ in $P$ let
$$f(Q) = [QV_1V_2] - [QV_2V_3] + [QV_3V_4] - \dots + (-1)^{n-1}[QV_nV_1],$$
(blue minus green). $Q$ is a balancing point iff $f(Q) = 0$.

**$f$ is affine.** For $Q$ in the convex polygon, $Q$ lies on the inner side of each edge $V_iV_{i+1}$, so $[QV_iV_{i+1}] = \frac12|V_iV_{i+1}|\cdot\operatorname{dist}(Q, \text{line } V_iV_{i+1})$, and this distance is an affine function of the coordinates of $Q$ on the inner side. Hence $f(Q) = \alpha x + \beta y + \gamma$ on $P$ for some constants.

**Zero set.** If $\alpha = \beta = 0$, then either no point or every point of $P$ is balancing; neither gives exactly one. Otherwise $\{f = 0\}$ is a line $\ell$, and the balancing points are exactly the points of $\ell \cap P$. This is a convex set, a single point by assumption. If $\ell$ passed through an interior point of $P$, it would contain a whole small segment of $P$ around that point. So $\ell$ meets $P$ only in boundary points: $\ell$ is a supporting line, and $\ell \cap P$ is either an edge or a vertex. An edge has more than one point, so $\ell \cap P$ is a single vertex.

Hence the unique balancing point is a vertex of $P$. ∎

*(The situation really occurs: the official solution notes that the hexagon with vertices $(0,0), (0,2), (1,10), (3,10), (4, \frac{14}3), (4, \frac83)$ has exactly one balancing point, the vertex $(0,0)$: its triangles have areas $0, 1, 10, 13, 4, 0$ and $0 - 1 + 10 - 13 + 4 - 0 = 0$.)*

usamts-2015-r1-04.title: Thresholds in each weight class
usamts-2015-r1-04.body:
The players are the pairs $(w, h)$ with $190 \le w < h \le 197$ (weight $w$, height $h$), i.e. 28 players.

**Shape of a team.** For a weight $w$, if $(w, h)$ is on the team then by (i) so is every $(w, h')$ with $h' \ge h$. So the team's players of weight $w$ are all those with height $\ge t_w$, for a threshold $t_w$ (or none). If weight class $w$ is used and $w' < w$, then $(w', t_w)$ is a player (since $t_w > w > w'$) who is at least as tall and lighter, so class $w'$ is used too, with $t_{w'} \le t_w$. Hence the used weights are $190, 191, \dots, 189 + j$ for some $0 \le j \le 7$, with
$$t_{190} \le t_{191} \le \dots \le t_{189+j} \le 197,$$
and conversely any such thresholds satisfy (i).

**Condition (ii).** The heights on the team are exactly $t_{190}, \dots, 197$ (class 190 has the smallest threshold), and the weights on the team are $190, \dots, 189 + j$. Condition (ii) says these sets are disjoint, i.e. $t_{190} \ge 190 + j$. (This also guarantees $t_w > w$ for each used $w$.)

**Count.** For fixed $j$ we need non-decreasing sequences of length $j$ with values in $\{190 + j, \dots, 197\}$, a set of $8 - j$ values. There are $\binom{(8 - j) + j - 1}{j} = \binom{7}{j}$ of them. So the number of teams is
$$\sum_{j=0}^{7}\binom7j = 2^7 = 128.$$

**Answer: 128**

usamts-2015-r1-04.title: Lattice paths (official idea)
usamts-2015-r1-04.body:
Plot players as lattice points (weight, height) in the triangle $190 \le x < y \le 197$. Rule (i) says a team is closed under moving up and to the left. Rule (ii) says that if the shortest team member of weight 190 has height $190 + m$, no one of weight $\ge 190 + m$ is on the team.

Record the team by the lowest chosen point $p_k$ in each used column $x = 190 + k$. These points form an up-right path from $p_0$ that ends, after extending it to height 198, at $(189 + m, 198)$. Such a path has $m - 1$ steps right and $7 - (m - 1)$ steps up, so there are $\binom{7}{m-1}$ teams for each $m = 1, \dots, 7$. Adding the empty team:
$$1 + \sum_{m=1}^{7}\binom{7}{m-1} = 1 + (2^7 - 1) = 128.$$
A direct computer enumeration also gives 128.

**Answer: 128**

usamts-2015-r1-05.title: Reduce to coprime terms
usamts-2015-r1-05.body:
**Multiples of 6 work:** $n = 6m$ has divisors $m, 2m, 3m$ in arithmetic progression with sum $6m$.

**Nothing else works.** Suppose $d_1 < d_2 < \dots < d_k$ ($k \ge 2$) are divisors of $n$ in arithmetic progression with sum $n$. Let $g = \gcd(d_1, \dots, d_k)$; then $\frac{d_i}{g}$ are divisors of $\frac ng$ in arithmetic progression with sum $\frac ng$. So it suffices to show that when the $d_i$ have no common factor, $n = 6$ (then the original $n = 6g$).

* *Consecutive terms are coprime:* a common divisor $r$ of $d_i, d_{i+1}$ divides the common difference, hence every term, so $r = 1$.
* *$k = 2$ is impossible:* $n = d_1 + d_2$ with $d_1 < d_2$ gives $\frac n2 < d_2 < n$, but a proper divisor of $n$ is at most $\frac n2$.
* *$k \ge 3$:* $d_{k-1}$ and $d_k$ are coprime divisors of $n$, so $d_{k-1}d_k \mid n$ and $n \ge d_{k-1}d_k \ge k\,d_{k-1}$ (as $d_k \ge k$ for $k$ distinct positive integers). For $k \ge 3$, $d_{k-1}$ is at least the average $\frac nk$ of the progression, so $k\,d_{k-1} \ge n$. Hence all inequalities are equalities: $d_{k-1}$ equals the average, which for an arithmetic progression happens only when $k = 3$, and $d_k = k = 3$. So $(d_1, d_2, d_3) = (1, 2, 3)$ and $n = 6$.

**Answer: all positive multiples of 6.** ∎
